newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia's Samper says too little profit in coffee.
newsitem.headline: Colombia's Samper says too little profit in coffee.

text.p: President Ernesto Samper conceded Monday that Colombia, one of the world's best coffee producers, is currently one of the worst places for growers to do business because of its sky-production costs.
"We cultivate the best varities and we're in the vanguard in terms of coffee investigation," Samper said in a speech to an annual meeting of coffee growers from across Colombia.
"But our production costs have long exceeded the level at which coffee-growing could become a reasonably profitable activity again," he said.

Samper did not spell out how to bring production costs down, however, saying only that there was a need for greater efficiency if Colombia was to compete on a more equal footing with other coffee-producing countries.

High costs are partly due to Colombia's exorbitant lending rates and inflation. But the bulk of growers' costs stem from manual labor, prompting Samper to suggest an eventual reduction in coffee acerage while maintaining production at current levels.
Coffee growers say their biggest problem, in terms of profitability, is the recent strengthening of the peso which has sharply eroded the value of export revenues in real peso terms.

The government has been widely criticized for failing to convince the central bank, which is autonomous and wholly responsible for monetary policy, to devalue the peso and help breathe new life into the export sector.
Samper said the government was a victim of the central bank's foreign exchange policy and not its "executioner," however.

The central bank likes a strong currency as a buffer against inflation and has steadfastly refused to alter the peso's daily floating rate exchange band. It finally agreed Friday to modify the band next year, however.

The decision, announced at a news conference by central bank chief Miguel Urrutia and Finance Minister Jose Antonio Ocampo, could lead to a targeted 15 to 29 percent devaluation of the peso in 1997 and Samper said exporters could look now look forward to "a more favorable framework in the coming year."
